items.question: Is string? a different type from string at run time?
items.answer: No. Nullable reference types are annotations. string and string? are the same CLR type. The compiler uses the annotation plus flow analysis to warn. int? is different: it is System.Nullable<int>, a value type with HasValue.
followUps: What happens when you box a null int??
Can you observe string? with reflection as a distinct type?
items.sixtySeconds: int? is Nullable<T>. string? is still String. NRT is compile-time. Boxing a null Nullable<T> becomes a null object.

items.question: Does enabling nullable reference types stop NullReferenceException?
items.answer: No. It changes diagnostics. Reflection, JSON deserializers, Redis GET misses, and SQS optional attributes can still produce null. You still write runtime guards at process boundaries.
followUps: Where would you put ThrowIfNull in an SQS batch handler?
When is the null-forgiving operator acceptable?
items.sixtySeconds: NRT is a warning system. Runtime null still exists. Guard public APIs; do not plaster ! on deserializer output.

items.question: How does this compare to TypeScript strictNullChecks?
items.answer: Both are compile-time. tsc erases; the C# compiler also does not emit a different string type for string?. The difference is Nullable<T> on value types, and the CLR still has real null references. JS undefined vs null is a third state TypeScript has to model; C# has one null plus HasValue on structs.
followUps: What is the analogue of ?., ??, and ! in TypeScript?
Does either system protect you after JSON.parse?
items.sixtySeconds: strictNullChecks ≈ NRT: warnings, not runtime. C# still has Nullable<T> and real NREs. JSON and Redis are unchecked at the boundary.

items.question: When do you use MaybeNull or NotNull instead of T??
items.answer: On generic APIs where T is unconstrained, T? is awkward. [return: MaybeNull] says Find can return default/null even if T is a non-nullable annotation. [NotNull] on a parameter says a helper that accepts T? leaves the value not-null after return, which is how ThrowIfNull is modeled.
followUps: What does NotNullWhen(true) do for TryGetValue-style methods?
Does required mean the property cannot be null?
items.sixtySeconds: Attributes refine generic and bool-returning contracts. required means initialized, not non-null. NotNullWhen is the Try* pattern.
